strang2016.citation: Strang, G. (2016). Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th edition. Wellesley-Cambridge Press. Chapter 1 (vectors, linear combinations, lengths and dot products) and chapters 2 and 8 (matrices, multiplication, linear transformations).
strang2016.read: table of contents and the free sample section 1.3; sections 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.4, 5.1 and 8.1 are not in the free samples, so those claims were checked on their mathematical merits, not against the book's text
claims: A matrix applied to a vector gives a combination of the matrix's columns, weighted by the vector's components; so the first column is where the first unit vector lands and the second column where the second lands (section 2.1).
A linear transformation keeps straight lines straight and sends the zero vector to zero (chapter 8).
A rotation by 90 degrees has columns (0, 1) and (-1, 0); a stretch along x by 2 has columns (2, 0) and (0, 1); a shear [[1, 1], [0, 1]] slides each row sideways by its height.
The determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix is the factor by which it scales areas; a shear has determinant 1.
Doing one transformation after another is multiplying their matrices, and matrix multiplication is not commutative in general: AB and BA can differ (section 2.4).
A product of linear transformations is again a linear transformation, so stacking matrices without anything between them gives one matrix.
strang2016.does_not_prove: Anything about language models; it is the mathematics the lesson uses.

ours-model.short: Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights
ours-model.citation: media/school/attention/model.json, read by tools/school/fill_matrices.mjs, which rebuilds the attention film's query, key and score from the layer-norm output and the head's slices of the query-key-value matrix, and refuses to write if they differ from the film's by more than 1e-4.
claims: Each layer has biases after its matrices (the query-key-value projection, the output projection and both MLP matrices).

At layer 2, head 2, the input (after layer normalisation) is 32 numbers; the head's query and key slices are 32 by 16 with 16 biases each; q . k = 41.28 and q . k / 4 = 10.32, the score the attention film shows.
The model's MLP uses GELU between its two matrices.
ours-model.interval: Not applicable: exact recomputation from stored weights.
ours-model.does_not_prove: Anything about how large models' query matrices behave.

vaswani2017.short: Vaswani and others 2017, Attention Is All You Need
vaswani2017.citation: Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, L., Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS 30.
claims: Queries, keys and values are made by multiplying the input by learned projection matrices, one set per head (section 3.2.2).
Scores are dot products of queries and keys divided by the square root of the key length (section 3.2.1).
The paper writes the attention projections as matrices without biases; our model's projections have biases.
vaswani2017.does_not_prove: How a particular trained model uses its projections.

ba2016.short: Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016, Layer Normalization
ba2016.citation: Ba, J. L., Kiros, J. R., Hinton, G. E. (2016). Layer Normalization. arXiv:1607.06450.
claims: Layer normalisation shifts each input's numbers to mean zero and scales them to unit spread, then applies a learned gain and bias, so the output's spread is set by the learned gain.
ba2016.does_not_prove: Why it helps in a particular model.

hendrycks2016.short: Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016, Gaussian Error Linear Units
hendrycks2016.citation: Hendrycks, D., Gimpel, K. (2016). Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs). arXiv:1606.08415.
claims: GELU is a smooth nonlinearity, x times the standard normal cumulative distribution at x, so it treats large, small and negative inputs differently.
Our model uses the paper's tanh approximation of GELU.
hendrycks2016.does_not_prove: That GELU is the best choice.
